newsitem.title: USA: Western Resources seen dropping ADT bid soon.
newsitem.headline: Western Resources seen dropping ADT bid soon.

text.p: Western Resources Inc. is expected soon to drop its $3.5 billion hostile bid for ADT Ltd. after a six-month effort that pushed the security giant into the arms of Tyco International Ltd.

The Kansas-based utility, which holds a 27 percent stake in ADT, may take the first step this week by cancelling a June 17 meeting at which shareholders are slated to vote on the bid. Although Western Resources said the meeting is still officially scheduled, it has not yet distributed proxy materials related to the session.
"I would not be surprised at all to see them drop the bid," said Andrew Jeffrey of Robertson, Stephens & Co.

The move would come as ADT proceeds with its planned $5.4 billion merger with Tyco. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this month cleared the proposed union, which was set after ADT rejected Western's unsolicited offer.

Western launched its takeover effort last December after slowly amassing the 27 percent stake in the Bermuda-based firm. The bid was widely considered too low for a company that is a key player in the booming electronic security industry.
ADT and Western then sued each other over the bid. A Bermuda court is set this week to consider one of the claims.
Although Western has refused to confirm that it is in negotiations to drop the takeover effort, ADT last month disclosed the development in a federal filing.
A Western spokeswoman declined to comment on the issue, saying only that the company has continually said it is reviewing its options. She did not elaborate.
A move by Western to withdraw its bid also would preserve accounting benefits associated with its planned $2 billion acquisition of Kansas City Power and Light Co.
Western struck a merger agreeement with KCP&L in February after a 10-month fight in which it wrested KCP&L from a planned merger with UtiliCorp United Inc.

But industry experts said Western could lose its ability to use pooling accounting in the KCP&L deal if it tried to sell its ADT holdings after ADT merges with Tyco. Companies involved in pooling transactions must follow strict rules in order to be eligible for the method in which buyers typically report higher earnings than those involved in purchase accounting transactions.
"I think that's the main reason, even though Western has said all along that a sale (of ADT holdings) would not reduce its ability to pool," said James Dobson of Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette.

Meanwhile, Western will not go home empty-handed if it drops its offer for ADT. Industry experts estimate its $600 million investment in ADT is now worth about $1 billion and the company is expected to move quickly to further boost its position in the growing electronic security business.
Western late last year bought the electronic security business of Westinghouse Electric Corp. for $368 million and has stressed it plans to expand in the industry.
"In this case, the loser is making a ton of money. Western does not have to get hold of ADT in order to become a major player in the security business," said Jeffrey Kessler of Lehman Brothers.
